title: Hotel booking system (reservations without double booking)
statement: Design a hotel booking system. Users search hotels by city and dates, see room types and prices, and book a room. Hotels can have very limited rooms on popular dates. The system must never sell the same room twice, payments go through an external provider, and both guests and hotels must see a confirmed booking quickly.

guide.gist: Agoda's core business, reported as a design round, an "architecture for booking processing" round and a REST round. The heart is **inventory per (hotel, room type, date)** and an atomic way to take it — then the **booking state machine** around a slow, failable payment. Search is read-heavy and cacheable; booking is write-light but must be correct.
clarify: Do we sell a specific room or a room type?
Room type per night is the usual model — inventory is a count per (hotel, room_type, date).
How many bookings per day, and how hot are the hottest hotels?

Pay now or pay at hotel? How long may a room be held during payment?

Is the price shown at search guaranteed at booking?

Does some inventory come from external suppliers?
If so, the supplier confirms the booking too — a two-step confirmation.
numbers: 1.5M bookings/day ≈ 17/s average, ~200/s peak — writes are small; correctness, not throughput, is the problem.
Searches are ~100× bookings → 2,000–20,000 searches/s; availability must be cached for search.
Inventory rows: 1M hotels × 5 room types × 365 days ≈ 1.8B rows → shard by hotel_id.

deep: Taking inventory atomically across nights

A 3-night stay needs one room on each of 3 dates. In one transaction: UPDATE inventory SET held = held + 1 WHERE hotel = ? AND room_type = ? AND date IN (…) AND total − sold − held > 0, and check that 3 rows changed; otherwise roll back. No distributed lock — the database row is the lock. Shard by hotel so all nights of one hotel are on one shard.
The booking state machine around payment

Hold the rooms (PENDING, TTL 15 min) → authorise payment → CONFIRMED (held becomes sold, capture later) or FAILED (release). Every transition is a conditional update on the booking's state, so a late payment callback and the expiry job cannot both win. Payment calls carry the booking id as their idempotency key.
Search vs booking consistency

Search reads a cached availability that can be seconds stale — that is fine, because booking re-checks with the conditional update. Say this out loud: search is eventually consistent, booking is strongly consistent, and the boundary is the quote.
Hot hotels on peak dates

A flash sale on one hotel makes one row hot. Options: keep the transaction tiny; queue bookings per hotel; or pre-split inventory into a few buckets. Usually the conditional update is enough at ~200 bookings/s total.
followups: Two guests book the last room at the same moment. What happens?
Both run the conditional update; the database serialises them on the row. One updates 1 row and holds the room, the other updates 0 rows and gets "sold out" before any payment.
Payment succeeded but our service crashed before confirming.

The payment provider's webhook (and a reconciliation job) finds the PENDING booking by id and confirms it — idempotently. If the hold already expired and the room is gone, refund automatically and alert.
The client times out and retries POST /bookings.
The Idempotency-Key returns the original booking instead of creating a second one or charging twice.
How do you scale to 10× bookings?
Shard inventory and bookings by hotel_id; the booking path stays one shard per booking. Search scales separately with caches and replicas.
How would you monitor it?
Booking success rate, time to CONFIRMED, holds expired vs confirmed, oversell detector (sold > total alarm), payment provider latency and errors, reconciliation mismatches.
mistakes: Checking availability with a SELECT and then inserting the booking (check-then-act).
A distributed lock around the whole booking flow.
Charging the card before the room is held.
Reading the booking primary for search traffic.
No expiry for holds — rooms stay blocked after abandoned payments.

title: Flight search API aggregating 20–200 external suppliers
statement:
Design a flight-search API that aggregates results from 20–200 external suppliers.

- Each supplier answers one route query at a time: source, destination, travel date, passengers, cabin class.
- Suppliers have different SLAs and protocols (JSON, SOAP/XML, Protobuf).
- Several suppliers can return the same flight: de-duplicate and show the cheapest fare.
- Some suppliers answer in under a second; others take several minutes.
- The UI must show results quickly, without waiting for every supplier.
- Supplier data stays valid for one hour.

guide.gist: The most reported Agoda design question. The boxes are easy (gateway, orchestrator, connectors, cache, streaming). What gets graded is the **time model** — a client deadline in seconds vs supplier calls that can run for minutes — and **failure and recovery across services**: a pod dies mid-stream, a connector dies with calls in flight, the cache is down. The candidate who was selected said exactly this: the follow-ups on failure were the hard part.
clarify: How many searches per second at peak, and how concentrated on popular routes?
Decides cache hit rate and how many supplier calls we make — calls are slow and often cost money.
What does "quickly" mean — first results in 1 s? A complete page in 3 s?
Decides streaming vs a single response, and the deadline we give the user.
Is the search price binding, or re-checked at booking?
If re-priced at booking, an hour-old cache is acceptable for search.
Do suppliers have rate limits or per-call cost?
Decides per-supplier budgets, bulkheads and coalescing identical searches.
Must late results (minutes) ever reach this user, or only future searches?
Decides whether late results update the open page or only fill the cache.
numbers: 2,000 searches/s peak; 70% on the top 500 routes → a 1-hour cache keyed by (route, date, pax, cabin) can serve most of them.
Cold search fans out to up to 200 suppliers → 400K supplier calls/s if nothing is cached and nothing is coalesced — impossible; the cache and request coalescing are the design.
A result set ≈ 200 offers × 1 KB = 200 KB; 1 hour of distinct searches (~1M keys) ≈ 200 GB → a Redis cluster, not one node.
api: POST /v1/searches {from, to, date, pax, cabin} → 202 {searchId}  (idempotent on the same query for a few seconds)
GET /v1/searches/{searchId}/stream  → SSE: offer.added / offer.updated / supplier.done / search.complete, each with an event id
GET /v1/searches/{searchId}/results?cursor=…  → the current de-duplicated snapshot (also the reconnect fallback)
parts: Auth, rate limits per client, routing. Terminates TLS and keeps SSE connections.
Creates the search, checks the cache, fans out to suppliers, merges and de-duplicates, decides when the result is "complete enough".
One adapter per supplier: protocol (JSON / SOAP / Protobuf), mapping to a canonical offer, auth, timeouts, retries, per-supplier rate limit and circuit breaker.
Each supplier call is a job, so slow calls do not hold an HTTP thread and survive pod or connector restarts.
Per-search result set (offers by canonical flight id) for the stream, plus a 1-hour cache of per-supplier results by route query.
Pushes deltas to the browser; any pod can serve a stream because state lives in the result store, not the pod.
At booking, re-price the chosen offer with its supplier.
deep: Two clocks: the user deadline vs supplier lifetimes

The **user** gets a deadline: first results by ~1 s, "complete enough" at ~3–5 s. The **supplier call** has its own lifetime (up to minutes, its SLA). The orchestrator never waits for the slowest supplier; it closes the user-facing search at the deadline and lets slow calls finish in the background, writing into the cache for the next search (and optionally an "offer.updated" event if the page is still open). This one idea answers three follow-ups.
De-duplication while streaming

Give every offer a **canonical flight id** — carrier + flight numbers + departure times + cabin (for connections, the whole itinerary). The result store is a map keyed by that id holding the cheapest fare. The stream sends **upserts by id**, not raw supplier rows, so the client replaces a card instead of adding a second one. To avoid visible reshuffling, buffer the first ~800 ms, send one sorted batch, then deltas.
Recovery: pods, connectors, cache

Make every hop **resumable**: the search state is in Redis, the supplier jobs are in Kafka, the stream has event ids. A dead SSE pod → the browser reconnects with Last-Event-ID to any pod, which replays from the result store. A dead connector → its jobs are redelivered to another connector (at-least-once; results are idempotent upserts). Cache down → fall back to live supplier calls with **tight per-supplier budgets** and coalescing, so we degrade to slower and partial, not to a supplier stampede.
Protecting suppliers and cost

Coalesce identical in-flight searches (one supplier call serves everyone asking for BKK→SIN on 24 Dec). Per-supplier concurrency limits (bulkheads) and circuit breakers. Measure **supplier calls per search** as a first-class metric.
followups: Results streamed before de-duplication show duplicates. How do you stay fast without that?
Upsert by canonical flight id in the result store and stream upserts, never raw rows. Batch the first ~800 ms so the first paint is already merged and sorted; later deltas replace cards in place.
How do you set customer-facing latency targets when suppliers differ?

Set the SLO on what the user sees — first offers p95 < 1.5 s, "complete" by 5 s — not on suppliers. Each supplier gets a timeout derived from that deadline and its own history; suppliers that miss it still finish into the cache. Track per-supplier p99 and contribution (how often it wins the cheapest fare).
The pod serving an SSE connection dies. Can another pod resume?

Yes, if pods are stateless: offers are in the result store with a version per search; every event carries an id. EventSource reconnects automatically with Last-Event-ID; the new pod replays everything after that id from the store.
1–2% of suppliers take minutes. How do you keep fast results and their late answers?

Close the user search at the deadline; the slow supplier job keeps running (it lives in the job queue, not in the request). When it returns, it writes into the 1-hour cache and the search's result store; an open page gets an offer.updated event, a new search gets it from cache.
The connector service goes down with calls in flight. What happens?

Jobs were committed to Kafka before the call; the consumer offset is committed only after the result is written. Another connector instance picks the job up and re-issues the call. Results are upserts by (search, supplier), so a duplicate call does no harm. The stream just sees that supplier arrive late.
The cache is unavailable for several minutes, then comes back. How does the system behave?

Circuit-break the cache client and go to suppliers directly, but within per-supplier budgets and with in-process coalescing — show partial results rather than overload suppliers. When it returns, do not mass-repopulate: refill lazily on demand, with jittered TTLs so keys do not all expire together later.
Which cache technology, and why?

Redis Cluster: TTLs per key, fast hash and sorted-set structures for the per-search result map and the sorted view, pub/sub or streams for live updates, replicas for availability. Memcached lacks the data structures; a local in-process cache is a small first tier for the hottest routes.
mistakes: Waiting for all suppliers before answering — latency becomes the slowest supplier.
Calling suppliers from the request thread, so a pod restart loses in-flight work.
Streaming raw supplier rows and de-duplicating on the client.
Sticky SSE connections with state in pod memory — a pod failure loses the search.
No per-supplier budgets: a cache outage turns into a self-inflicted DDoS on suppliers.

title: Payment gateway for Agoda users at 10M DAU (with an external provider and reconciliation)
statement: Design the payment system for Agoda: at 10M daily active users, users pay for hotel and flight bookings. Payments go through external providers such as Stripe or Adyen. Cover the transaction flow, failures and retries, refunds, and a reconciliation system that makes sure our records and the provider's records agree.
why: A 2026 Staff report, in the "Data Management" architecture round. Money, idempotency and reconciliation are exactly what Staff is graded on.

guide.gist: The 2026 Staff report put this in the "Data Management" architecture round. The money must be **exactly once from the user's point of view** even though networks, providers and our services fail. That means: a **payment state machine**, **idempotency keys** end to end, a **double-entry ledger** as the source of truth, and **reconciliation** against the provider's settlement files. Throughput is modest; correctness and auditability are everything.
clarify: Authorise at booking and capture later, or charge immediately?
Hotels often authorise now and capture at check-in or confirmation — two-phase states.
How many payments per day, and how many currencies and providers?
Decides routing, FX handling and how many settlement files we reconcile.
Do we store card data?
No — tokenise with the provider so we stay out of most PCI scope.
Refunds and partial refunds? Chargebacks?
More states and ledger entries.
How fast must reconciliation flag a mismatch?
Daily settlement files vs near-real-time webhooks.
numbers: 10M DAU, ~5% book → 500K payments/day ≈ 6/s average, ~60/s peak — tiny for a database.
Each payment ≈ 5–10 ledger entries (auth, capture, fees, FX, refund) → ~5M ledger rows/day, ~2B/year → partition by month.
Provider calls p99 ≈ 1–3 s and fail ~0.1–1% transiently → retries and timeouts are the normal case, not the edge case.
api: POST /v1/payments  Idempotency-Key  {bookingId, amount, currency, paymentMethodToken} → {paymentId, status}
POST /v1/payments/{id}/capture · POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds {amount}  (each idempotent)
POST /webhooks/{provider}  (signed) → provider events: authorised, captured, failed, refunded, chargeback
parts: Validates, enforces the Idempotency-Key, creates the payment intent.
CREATED → AUTHORISING → AUTHORISED → CAPTURED / FAILED / REFUNDED; every transition conditional.
Chooses Stripe / Adyen / local methods by country, currency and health; one adapter each.
Every money movement is two balanced entries; append-only; the source of truth for balances.
payment.authorised etc. to the booking service and finance.
Verifies signatures, de-duplicates by provider event id, drives the state machine.
Matches our ledger against provider reports and settlement files; opens cases for mismatches.
deep: Idempotency end to end

The client sends an Idempotency-Key; we store it unique with the request hash and the result. Our call to the provider carries **our** payment id as the provider's idempotency key. So a retry at any hop — browser, our service, the provider call — maps to the same payment and the same provider charge.
Unknown outcomes

A timeout from the provider does not mean failure. Mark the payment UNKNOWN, never retry with a new key, and resolve by querying the provider by our id, by its webhook, or by reconciliation. The user sees "processing", not a second charge.
The ledger

Double-entry: debit customer receivable, credit provider clearing, and so on; entries are immutable, corrections are new entries. Balances are sums, so they can be audited and rebuilt. Store amounts as integer minor units with a currency.
Reconciliation

Three-way: our ledger, provider events/API, and the provider's settlement file (what money actually moved, minus fees). Match by our payment id; categorise mismatches (missing on our side, missing on theirs, amount or currency differs, timing). Auto-fix the safe ones (a missed webhook), queue the rest for finance.
followups: The provider times out on a charge. Do you retry?
Not blindly. Retry only with the same provider idempotency key; or query the provider by our payment id first. Until we know, the payment is UNKNOWN.
A webhook arrives twice, or before our API call returns.
De-duplicate by provider event id; transitions are conditional (only AUTHORISING → AUTHORISED), so order and duplicates do not matter.
How do you switch providers when one is down?
Health-based routing per region; new payments go to the backup. In-flight ones stay with their provider — never re-charge a payment elsewhere without knowing the first outcome.
Where does strong consistency matter, and where not?
The payment state and ledger: strong, one database, transactions. Analytics, emails, dashboards: async from the outbox.
How would you monitor it?
Authorisation success rate per provider and country, provider latency, UNKNOWN count and age, webhook lag, reconciliation mismatch count and value, refunds and chargebacks.
A user pays $200 with a $20 coupon and $30 store credit. How is that one payment?

One checkout, three tenders: the coupon is reserved, the store credit is held in the ledger, and the card is authorised for $150. Card success captures all three; any failure releases all three. Each tender is a leg under one payment, so a refund later knows exactly what to give back to where.
Your team owns refunds too. How does this design make refunds easy?

Refunds reuse the same pieces: legs per tender, idempotency per leg, the ledger's cap (refunded ≤ captured), the same provider adapters and the same reconciliation. If payment has no legs and no ledger, refunds become guesswork.
Who pays for a coupon discount — Agoda or the hotel?

It depends on the promotion's funding (Agoda-funded, hotel-funded or split). Record the funding on the promotion and post it to the ledger at capture, so the payout to the hotel and the marketing cost are both right without a later manual adjustment.

deep: A saga with an external system

Each step has a compensation: cancel the PNR if payment fails, refund if ticketing fails permanently. The orchestrator persists each step, so a crash resumes from the last step. Every external call carries our booking reference so retries are safe.
Concurrent seat booking

A seat is a row (flight_id, seat_no, state, booking_id, held_until). Taking it: UPDATE … SET state = HELD WHERE flight_id = ? AND seat_no = ? AND (state = FREE OR held_until < now). One winner; the other gets 409 and picks again. The airline confirms the final assignment.
Unknown outcomes from the airline
A timeout on "create PNR" may have created it. Retry with the same reference, or query by reference before trying again; reconciliation cancels orphan PNRs.
Peak protection
Airline APIs have strict limits. Queue booking steps per airline with a token bucket; show users a fair waiting state rather than failing randomly.
followups: Payment succeeded, but ticketing failed.
Retry ticketing within the hold window; if it fails permanently, void or refund automatically and tell the user — the saga's compensation for that step.

The airline call times out on hold creation.

Find the issues in this existing design: booking service calls airline, then payment, then writes the DB.
No persisted saga state (a crash loses track of a paid booking), payment before a confirmed hold, no idempotency, the DB written last so retries duplicate. Fix the order and persist each step.

Booking funnel per step, saga steps stuck per state, airline latency and errors, PNR orphans, refunds due to ticketing failures.

guide.gist: Reported as a 2026 Staff platform/system-design round that the candidate did not clear. The load is tiny (~2 req/s), so the question is **judgement**: keep partners **off the core booking path**, give them a **read model** fed by events, design a **cursor / sync-token API** instead of time-window queries, enforce **per-supplier isolation and auth**, and say what you would *not* build at this scale.
clarify: How fresh must supplier data be?
Seconds → CDC/events into a read model; minutes → a replica is enough.
Why do suppliers poll windows — what are they trying to do?
Usually "give me what changed" → an incremental sync token answers it better.
How large are the biggest suppliers' result sets?
Decides pagination and page size.

Then an ack endpoint and redelivery.

deep: Why not call the internal Booking API

Every supplier query would load the service that takes bookings — the money path — and couple external contracts to internal ones. A separate read path means a supplier's backfill can never slow checkout.
Sync tokens instead of time windows

"Last 5 minutes" polled every minute either overlaps or misses rows (clock skew, late commits). A sync token encodes the last (updated_at, id) seen; the API returns rows strictly after it, reading slightly behind the newest commit. No duplicates, no gaps, any polling interval.
Replica vs CDC read model

A read replica is the cheapest first step and fine at 2 req/s. A CDC-fed read model adds supplier-specific indexes, denormalised fields and no load on the primary at all. Phase it: replica now, read model if queries get heavy or the schema should be decoupled.
Isolation and security
The supplier id comes from the token, never the request. Per-supplier quotas. PII minimised in responses. Audit every access.
followups: Isn't CDC overkill for 2 req/s?
Yes as a first step — start with a replica and a separate deployment; CDC is the step when we need freshness without primary load or a decoupled schema.
A supplier misses a day and wants to catch up.
Its last sync token still works; the change log or read model is retained ≥ 30 days.

/v1 path, additive changes only, deprecation windows; contract tests per supplier.
A supplier hammers the API.
Per-supplier rate limit with 429 and Retry-After; quotas; tell them about sync tokens.
How would you monitor it?
Requests and 429s per supplier, read-model lag behind the primary, p99 latency, auth failures, webhook delivery success.

Trusting a supplier id in the body.
Building Kafka, CQRS and sharding for 2 requests a second.

guide.gist: Reported as "hotel booking/search like Booking.com with emphasis on proximity search", plus a ranking question. Then a **two-stage ranking**: cheap retrieval, then a model on the top few hundred.
clarify: Search by city, by map area, by distance from a point — all three?
Decides geo queries: a city filter, a bounding box, a radius.
Must results show only available hotels for the dates?
Decides whether availability is a filter in retrieval or a check after.

Minutes stale is usual; exact at the hotel page and booking.

p99 ~300–500 ms for the results page.
Personalised ranking?
Adds user features to the ranker; keep retrieval generic.
numbers: 2M+ properties; 20,000 searches/s at peak.
A city like Bangkok has ~10K properties — retrieval returns hundreds, ranking scores ~500.

Per hotel: a compact calendar of availability and a min price per night, updated from inventory and pricing events.

deep: Proximity search

Store each hotel's location as a geo_point; the index supports radius and bounding-box queries using a geohash / BKD tree under the hood. Conceptually: a geohash turns lat/long into a string where shared prefixes mean nearby, so "within 3 km" becomes a few prefix cells to scan, then an exact distance check. Rank by distance only when the user sorts by distance; otherwise distance is a feature.
Availability without slowing search

Do not index availability per night as documents. Retrieve by geo and static filters, then check the top N against an availability cache (a bitmap or calendar per hotel and room type), dropping unavailable ones; over-fetch to keep a full page. Exact availability is checked again on the hotel page and at booking.
Two-stage ranking

Stage 1: retrieval with cheap scoring (text match, distance, review score) → ~500 candidates. Stage 2: a model scores each with richer features (price competitiveness, historic click-through and conversion for this hotel and market, user preferences). Log impressions and clicks to train it; A/B test changes.
Prices that change
Show a cached "from" price on the list; fetch live prices for the visible page asynchronously; never promise a price before the hotel page re-prices.
followups: How do geohashes handle points near a cell border?

How do you rank fairly for new hotels with no history?
Priors from similar hotels, exploration slots, and down-weighting history features until there is data.
Latency is 2 s in Bangkok at peak. Where do you look?
Per-stage timings: index query, availability check, ranker; usually over-fetch size or the ranker's feature fetches — cache features, cap candidates.
How do you keep the index fresh?
Change events (property, rating, amenities) → indexer → near-real-time index refresh; availability and price stay outside the index.
How would you measure ranking quality?
Conversion and click-through by position, NDCG offline, A/B tests online, and guardrails on latency.

title: Hotel inventory and availability (internal hotels + external suppliers)
statement: Design the hotel inventory and availability system. Some hotels manage their rooms directly with us (they update counts and rates in our extranet or through a channel manager); others come from external suppliers and partners whose inventory we must query or receive. Searches need fast availability; bookings must never oversell; and the data from different sources must stay consistent.
why: Merging internal and external availability without overselling.

variants.source: codingkaro — Senior, Bangkok, Jun 2025 (via search summary)
variants.text: Hotel inventory system design: find the inventory of hotels by querying Agoda's internal data and calling external services (MakeMyTrip, Booking.com) for their inventory.
Design a hotel inventory availability system on a virtual whiteboard.

guide.gist: The hard part is **two kinds of truth**. For direct hotels **we** own the count, so a conditional update is the truth. For supplier inventory **they** own it, so ours is a cache that can be wrong — booking must confirm with the supplier. On top: ingesting many rate/availability updates from channel managers, and serving availability fast.

Can the same hotel come from several sources?
Then we map to one canonical hotel and pick the best source per booking.
Do rates vary by length of stay, occupancy, cancellation policy?
Decides the rate-plan model.

title: Coupon and promotion system for flash sales (limited redemptions at peak)
statement: Design a coupon and promotion system. Marketing creates promotions (percent or fixed discounts, with rules such as minimum spend, destination, user segment, dates) and coupon codes, some with a limited number of uses. During a flash sale, a very large number of users try to redeem the same limited codes at the same moment. Prevent overselling and abuse, and keep checkout fast.
why: A 2026 report plus two prep guides (flash sale, concert booking): limited stock under a spike.

variants.text: Design a coupon system.
A high-throughput coupon and promotion service that prevents race conditions at peak volume.
variants.note: A prep guide's list, not a first-hand report.

variants.source: LeetCode 7082771 — Staff, Bangkok, Jul–Aug 2025 — not counted
variants.text: Platform round: an existing booking design to improve; one variant resembled a flash sale applied to concert bookings (load balancer, rate limiter, message queue).
variants.note: Platform round; the promo drill on the platform page covers it.

variants.text: Commonly reported prompts: Concert Booking System, Flash Sale System.
variants.note: A prep guide; folded in here because the hard part is the same (limited stock under a spike).

guide.gist: Reported in 2026 as "design a coupon system", and listed by guides as a flash-sale / race-condition question. Two halves: a **rules engine** (is this promotion valid for this cart?) that must be fast and read-mostly, and a **limited counter** under a spike that must not oversell. The trick is to make redemption a **reservation that expires**, decremented atomically, with one durable source of truth.
clarify: Must exactly N redemptions happen, or is about N fine?
Exact needs one authoritative counter; approximate allows sharded counters.
One use per user? Stackable with other promotions?
Unique constraints and a stacking policy.
When is a code consumed — at apply, at booking, at payment?
Usually reserved at booking, consumed at payment success.
How big is the spike?
e.g. 100K users in a minute for a 1,000-use code — decides Redis in front.
Who creates promotions and how fast must changes apply?
Admin API; propagate in seconds via cache invalidation.
numbers: Flash sale: 100K users in 60 s on one code → ~1,700 redemption attempts/s on one key, 99% of them must fail fast.
Normal checkout: ~200 bookings/s, each evaluates ~20 candidate promotions → 4,000 rule evaluations/s — cache promotions in memory.
Redemption records: 5M/day → partition by date.

parts: Create and edit promotions and codes; validation and audit.
Evaluates eligibility against the cart and user; promotions cached in memory, refreshed on change.
Reserve → confirm / release / expire; one per user enforced by a unique key.
Redis for the fast atomic decrement at flash time; the database records every redemption.
Rate limits per user, device and IP; bot detection on hot codes.
deep: An atomic, fast decrement

A Lua script in Redis: if remaining > 0 and the user has not used it, decrement and record the reservation; otherwise reject. One round trip, atomic, ~100K ops/s on one key. Every success also writes a redemption row (unique on code + user); a reconciler compares Redis with the database.
Reservations that expire

A reservation holds a use for ~15 minutes while the user pays. Payment success confirms it; failure or timeout releases it (increment back). Expiry makes compensation automatic instead of best-effort.
Source of truth

For money-like limits, the database is authoritative (Redis can lose recent writes on failover). Rebuild Redis from confirmed + active reservations after a failover; if exactness matters more than speed, use a conditional database update (remaining > 0) and accept lower peak throughput.
Rules at scale
Promotions change rarely and are read constantly: load them into each instance's memory, index by destination and segment, invalidate by event. Evaluating is a pure function — easy to test and fast.
followups: Redis fails over during the flash sale.
A few reservations may be lost from Redis; the database still has them. Pause the code for seconds, rebuild the count from the database, resume — oversell avoided at the cost of a short pause.
How do you stop one user redeeming many times with many accounts?
Per-device and per-payment-instrument limits, velocity rules, risk scoring; one use per verified account.
The spike is 1M users for 100 codes.
Put a queue / waiting room in front, or a lottery; most requests should be rejected at the edge from a local "sold out" flag once the count hits zero.
Two promotions apply. Which wins?
A stacking policy as data: exclusive groups and priority; the engine picks the best allowed combination.
How would you monitor it?
Redemptions per second, remaining count, reservation expiries, Redis vs DB drift, rejection reasons, abuse blocks.
The booking is cancelled. Does the user get the coupon back?

Policy as data: restore if the cancellation is free and the coupon has not expired; otherwise forfeit. Restoring is a redemption status change (confirmed → released) plus a counter increment — never cash. The refund service asks the coupon service, it does not decide.
Finance asks how much the flash sale cost and who funded it.

Each redemption records the discount amount and the funding split; capture posts it to the ledger (marketing expense or hotel-funded payable reduction). The cost is a ledger query, reconciled daily against redemptions.
How do coupons and store credit interact?
Apply coupons to the price first, then tenders. A refund reverses in the opposite order. Stacking rules sit in the promotion engine, not in checkout.
mistakes: Decrementing in Redis and updating the DB as two separate best-effort steps.
Consuming the code at validation time, before payment.
A distributed lock around a single counter.
Evaluating rules by querying the database per request.
No per-user uniqueness.
guide.say: "Promotions live in memory for a pure rules engine; redemption is an expiring reservation taken by one atomic Redis script with a unique row per user in the database as the truth; payment confirms or releases it; and a reconciler plus a local sold-out flag keep the flash sale correct and fast."

title: Booking reconciliation with external partner platforms
statement: External platforms (partners and suppliers) create hotel bookings through Agoda's APIs. Booking activity is stored on both sides: in Agoda's systems and in the partner's. Design a reconciliation system that finds and resolves differences — missing bookings, wrong statuses, different amounts — between the two.
why: The candidate who got it was rejected for missing edge cases — prepare it deliberately.

variants.text: Round 2: a reconciliation system — Agoda exposes APIs that external platforms use for hotel bookings; booking activity is stored on both sides.
variants.note: "Produced a design but missed many edge cases — little grounding in reconciliation systems." Rejected.

guide.gist: The candidate who got this was rejected for "missing many edge cases". So the answer is mostly **the edge cases, made systematic**: a canonical record, a reliable way to get the partner's data (files or APIs), **matching** by keys with tolerances, **categorising** every mismatch, **time windows** for in-flight bookings, and a **case workflow** that closes each one. Volume is modest; precision and auditability matter.
clarify: How do we get the partner's data — daily files, an API, or their webhooks?
Decides batch vs continuous reconciliation.
What is the shared key — our booking id, their reference, both?
Without a shared key, matching needs fuzzy rules.
What fields must agree — status, dates, amount, currency, guest?
Decides the comparison and tolerances (FX rounding).
Who fixes mismatches — automatically or a team?
Decides auto-resolution rules and a case queue.
How quickly must a difference be found?
Daily is common; near-real-time for high-value partners.
numbers: 50 partners × ~20K bookings/day each = 1M records/day per side.
A typical healthy mismatch rate is 0.1–1% → 1K–10K cases/day; most must auto-resolve.
Bookings change for weeks (modifications, cancellations) → reconcile on a rolling window, not one day.

deep: Matching

Primary key: our booking id echoed by the partner; fallback: their reference; last resort: fuzzy (hotel + dates + guest name + amount). Compare status, dates, room, amount and currency with tolerances (FX rounding within 0.01). Every pair gets a label: MATCH, MISSING_OURS, MISSING_THEIRS, STATUS_DIFF, AMOUNT_DIFF, DATE_DIFF, DUPLICATE.
Edge cases that sink this question

In-flight bookings (created at 23:59 on one side, 00:01 on the other — use a grace window). Modifications and cancellations after the file was cut. Time zones of the cut-off. Duplicates on one side. Partial refunds. Currency conversions. Late files and re-sent files (idempotent ingestion by file checksum). A missing whole file looks like "everything missing" — detect it before matching.
Rolling windows and state
Reconcile each booking until it is final (stay completed and paid) plus a margin, not only on its creation day. Keep the last known state of each pair, so tomorrow's run only re-checks what changed.
Resolution and audit
Auto-fix through the normal APIs (never by editing tables), record who/what/why, and re-check in the next run. Unresolved cases age and escalate.
followups: The partner sends no shared id.

A file arrives twice, or late.
Ingest idempotently by checksum and run id; a late file triggers a re-run of that window.
Real-time reconciliation for top partners?
Consume their webhooks and our booking events into a streaming matcher with a time window; the daily batch remains the safety net.
How do you avoid alert fatigue?
Categories with expected rates per partner; alert on rate changes, not on each case.
How would you monitor it?
Mismatch rate per partner and category, auto-resolved share, case age, files missing or late, run duration.
Your team reconciles payments. What are the three reconciliations?

Our payments vs the provider's settlement report (did the money move?); the provider's settlement vs the bank statement (did it arrive?); our ledger vs bookings (did every booking get paid, refunded or voided?). Each is the same engine: normalise, match on a key, classify, open cases.
A refund appears in the provider report but not in our system.

Classify as 'missing on our side'. Most likely a refund made in the provider's dashboard by support. Create the ledger entries from the report with an audit reason, and close the gap that allowed a manual refund outside the system.
Amounts differ by a few cents across thousands of rows.
Usually FX or rounding. Compare in integer minor units in the charged currency; tolerance rules are explicit per currency and per provider, and anything outside them is a case.
mistakes: Matching on one day's data and calling everything else missing.
Ignoring modifications and cancellations after creation.
Comparing amounts without currency and rounding rules.
Fixing data directly in the database without an audit trail.
Not detecting a missing or truncated partner file.

deep: Why not 2PC, and what instead

Two-phase commit needs every participant up and holds locks until the coordinator decides; a coordinator failure can block participants. Microservices use a **saga**: local transactions plus compensations, coordinated by an orchestrator whose state is durable. Guarantees come from idempotency + outbox + retries (at-least-once delivery, exactly-once effect).
Isolation levels and locking

InnoDB's default is REPEATABLE READ: plain SELECTs read a snapshot (no lock), so "SELECT then UPDATE" is a lost-update risk. Use a conditional UPDATE (atomic), or SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside the transaction (locks the row; with REPEATABLE READ also gap locks on ranges), or optimistic locking with a version column. Keep transactions short; never call another service inside one.
Indexes for the hot paths

A B+tree index on (hotel_id, room_type, date) makes the hold a range on one index; the booking lookup by idempotency key needs a UNIQUE index (it is also the duplicate check). A composite index serves the leftmost prefix; order the columns by equality first, range last. Covering indexes avoid reading the row. Every index costs write time — do not index everything.
Redis: what it is good for here

Single-threaded command execution makes INCR, SET NX PX and Lua scripts atomic. Good for: caches, rate limits, short holds. As a lock: SET key token NX PX 10000, release only if the token matches (Lua) — but a paused client can outlive its lease, so the protected resource must check a **fencing token** (monotonic number). Persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF) and async replication mean a failover can lose recent writes — so Redis is not the source of truth for bookings or money.
followups: Payment authorised, then the inventory hold expired. What does the saga do?
Compensate: void the authorisation, mark the booking failed, tell the user; or re-try the hold if inventory remains. Decided in the saga's state machine, not ad hoc.
How do you guarantee an event is published exactly once?
You cannot guarantee delivery exactly once; you make the effect exactly once: outbox (no lost events) + idempotent consumers (duplicates ignored).
Explain a deadlock in MySQL and how to avoid it.
Two transactions lock rows in opposite orders; InnoDB detects it and rolls one back. Lock in a consistent order (e.g. by date ascending), keep transactions short, retry on deadlock errors.
When would you use SELECT … FOR UPDATE instead of a conditional update?
When the decision needs several reads before writing (complex rules). Otherwise a single conditional update is simpler and holds the lock for less time.
Is Redlock safe?
Not on its own for correctness — timing assumptions break under pauses. Use fencing tokens checked by the resource, or keep the invariant in the database.
Booking, payment, coupon and store credit are four services. How do they commit together?

They don't — each one holds an expiring reservation (inventory hold, payment authorisation, coupon reservation, credit hold). The orchestrator confirms all of them after payment succeeds and releases all of them on failure or timeout. Expiry is the safety net if the orchestrator dies.
mistakes: Proposing 2PC across microservices.
Publishing to Kafka after the DB commit in application code (dual write).
SELECT then UPDATE under REPEATABLE READ without a lock or condition.
Calling another service while holding a database transaction open.
Using Redis as the booking store or a lock without fencing.

title: Tags from hotel reviews, searchable ("good location" → top 10 hotels)
statement: Hotel guest reviews are stored in a SQL database, arriving at about 500 review comments per second. Design a system that generates tags from the reviews ("good location", "clean rooms", "noisy", "great breakfast") and uses them in search: a query like "good location" should return the top 10 hotels for that tag, fast. Tags must stay up to date as new reviews arrive.
why: An Agoda-specific HLD: tags from guest reviews that power search. Very likely to be a team's real problem.

variants.text: A system that reads hotel guest reviews from a SQL database (~500 review comments/s) and generates tags from them; the tags power search — "good location" should return the top 10 matching hotels.
variants.note: Posted as "recently asked in Agoda interview"; no worked solution in the thread.

guide.gist: An Agoda HLD question from LeetCode Discuss. Three pieces: **getting reviews out of the SQL database without hurting it** (CDC), an **asynchronous tagging pipeline** (an NLP model, batched), and a **per-tag ranking** that is cheap to read (a pre-computed top-K per tag, not a query over all reviews). The interesting decisions are how a hotel's tag score is defined (count? share? recency? confidence?) and how it is updated incrementally.
clarify: Is the tag list fixed (a taxonomy) or discovered from text?
A fixed taxonomy (~200 tags) is far simpler to rank and translate; discovery is a research problem.
Which languages?
Decides the model — multilingual, or translate first.
How fresh must tags be?
Minutes is usual — so a stream, not a nightly batch, but no need for milliseconds.
"Top 10 for good location" — globally, or within a city and dates?
Almost always within a city or area — so rank per (tag, city).
Do negative mentions count ("location was not good")?
Yes — the model outputs sentiment per aspect, not just keywords.
numbers: 500 reviews/s ≈ 43M/day. A batched transformer model on GPUs does ~1–2K short texts/s per GPU → a few GPUs, with headroom.

Search for a tag ≈ thousands/s; reading a pre-computed list is O(1) — never compute it at query time.

deep: Defining a fair score

Raw counts favour big hotels. Use a share with a confidence correction: e.g. a Wilson lower bound on (positive mentions / total mentions of that aspect), multiplied by a recency decay. A hotel with 3 out of 3 positive mentions should not beat one with 900 out of 1,000.
Incremental updates

Each tagged review increments counters for (hotel, tag) and recomputes that hotel's score; then ZADD into the (tag, city) sorted set. Decay can be applied lazily (store the last-update time and decay on read) or by a periodic job.
Model in the pipeline

Batch requests to the model for throughput; keep the model version on each result; a new model triggers a backfill that writes to a new index version, then switches over (blue/green) — never mix versions in one ranking.
Protecting the source DB
Reading 500 rows/s with polling queries competes with writes; CDC from the binlog costs almost nothing and gives ordered, complete changes.
followups: A new model version changes everything. How do you roll it out?
Backfill into a new index version, compare quality offline and on a slice of traffic, then switch the alias; keep the old one for rollback.

title: "X people are viewing this hotel right now" (live viewer count)
statement: On a hotel page, Agoda shows "12 people are looking at this hotel right now". Design the system behind it: count, for every hotel page, how many distinct users are viewing it at the moment, and show the number on the page, updating it while the user stays. Millions of users browse at peak.

guide.gist: An Agoda first-round system design question from LeetCode Discuss. It looks small and is mostly about **defining "viewing now"** (a heartbeat within a time window), **counting distinct users per page cheaply** at high write rates, and **not over-engineering**: the number need not be exact, but it must not be misleading. Good answers pick sliding windows with heartbeats, a sharded in-memory counter, and polling or a cheap push.
clarify: What counts as "viewing now" — page open in the last 1 minute? 5?
Defines the window; drives everything else.
Exact or approximate?
Approximate within a few percent is fine — enables cheap structures.
How often must the number refresh on the page?
Every 30–60 s is enough; real-time push is optional.
Distinct users or page views?
Distinct users (or devices) — one user with 3 tabs counts once.
Is it shown for every hotel?
Maybe only above a threshold ("3+ viewing"), which also hides noise.
numbers: 2M concurrent users, one heartbeat every 30 s → ~67K heartbeats/s.
Active hotel pages at once: ~200K. Per hotel we need the distinct viewers in the last 60 s.
Reads ≈ heartbeats (each page reads its count when it heartbeats) — combine both in one call.

deep: Sliding window with a sorted set

Key presence:{hotel}. Heartbeat: ZADD key now session; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key 0 (now − 60 s); ZCARD key → count. Three commands in one pipeline/Lua script, O(log n). Memory ≈ active viewers × ~50 bytes — tens of MB.

Bucket by minute: a HyperLogLog per (hotel, minute) with PFADD session; the count = PFCOUNT over the last 2 buckets merged. Fixed ~12 KB per key, ~1% error, no per-session members to expire — TTL the bucket keys.
Hot hotels and sharding
Shard Redis by hotel_id. One very hot hotel is still only a few hundred writes/s — fine for one Redis shard. Client-side jitter on heartbeats avoids synchronised spikes.
Honesty and product rules
The number must not be fabricated or inflated (consumer-protection regulators have acted on fake urgency messages). Show it only above a threshold, round it, and count real distinct users.

A heartbeat every 30 s with the count in the response is far cheaper and good enough; push is optional for a live feel.

statement: Design a video platform like YouTube: registered users upload videos; any user can search for videos and watch them. Videos must play smoothly on different devices and network speeds, worldwide.
why: Reported with a rejection for shallow depth — practise going deep on transcoding and delivery.

variants.note: "I didn't explain the HLD in depth" — rejected after this round. Lesson: depth over breadth.

guide.gist: Reported as an Agoda HLD round where the candidate was **rejected for not going deep enough** — so breadth is not the bar. Go deep on the three hard parts: **upload and transcoding** (a resumable upload to object storage, then a DAG of transcode jobs into adaptive bitrate renditions), **delivery** (CDN with HLS/DASH segments — the main cost and latency lever), and **metadata + search** (a separate index). View counts are a classic follow-up.
clarify: Scale: uploads per day, views per day?
e.g. 500K uploads/day, 1B views/day — decides storage and CDN egress.
Max video size and length?
Decides resumable/chunked upload.
Live streaming in scope?
Usually not — say it.

Private / unlisted videos?

1B views/day × ~50 MB watched ≈ 50 PB/day egress → almost all must come from the CDN edge.
Transcoding: 500K videos × ~5 min × 5 renditions — a large, elastic worker pool (spot instances).

deep: Upload and processing

Direct-to-storage multipart upload (resumable; our servers never proxy bytes). An upload-complete event starts a workflow: split the video into chunks (GOP-aligned), transcode chunks in parallel per rendition (240p…1080p, several codecs), then package into HLS/DASH segments with manifests. The workflow is persisted (retries per chunk), so a failed worker redoes one chunk, not the whole video.
Adaptive streaming
The player downloads a manifest listing renditions; it fetches 2–6 s segments and switches bitrate as bandwidth changes. Segments are immutable files — perfect for CDN caching with long TTLs.
CDN and cost
Egress is the biggest cost. Popular videos are cached at the edge; the long tail is served from regional caches or origin. Pre-warm the edge for videos that start trending.
View counts
A view event goes to Kafka; a stream job aggregates per video per minute and updates the count; dedupe obvious repeats. Never UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 per view on the main DB.

Multipart upload resumes from the last completed part; the client retries only missing parts.

Upload success, time to playable, transcode queue depth, CDN hit ratio, playback start time and rebuffer rate.

Transcoding a whole video on one machine with no chunk retries.
Serving video from the origin instead of a CDN.
One rendition for every device.
Updating a view counter row per view.

statement: Design a chat application like WhatsApp: one-to-one and group messaging, delivery and read receipts, online/last-seen status, and messages delivered to users who were offline when they were sent. Users may have several devices.
why: Two reports: design WhatsApp (2024) and a chat app with read receipts and a SQL schema (intern round).

variants.text: Round 3 (architecture/platform): design WhatsApp.
variants.note: Also supplied by you.

variants.source: LeetCode 8419900 — SWE intern, 2nd round (also summarised on Glassdoor)
variants.text: Design a chat application with one-to-one and one-to-many messaging and read receipts; started from requirements, then built a SQL schema with a few hints. The round also asked what Docker is and why it is used.

guide.gist: The classic: **persistent connections** (WebSockets) to many gateway servers, a **routing layer** that knows which server holds each user's connection, a **message store** ordered per conversation, and **store-and-forward** for offline users with acknowledgements driving delivered/read receipts. Groups add fan-out.
clarify: How many users and messages per day?
e.g. 500M DAU, 50B messages/day → ~600K msgs/s.
Group size limit?
e.g. 1,024 — decides fan-out on write.
End-to-end encryption in scope?
Changes what the server can store (ciphertext only).
Message history on the server, or only until delivered?
WhatsApp-style deletes after delivery; others keep history.
Multi-device?
Each device is a delivery target with its own ack.
numbers: 50B messages/day ≈ 580K/s average, ~1.5M/s peak.
500M concurrent connections ÷ ~500K connections per gateway box ≈ 1,000 gateway servers.
100 B average message → ~5 TB/day if stored.
api: WebSocket: send {clientMsgId, convId, body} → ack {serverMsgId, seq}
Server → client: message {convId, seq, from, body}; client → server: delivered/read {convId, seq}
GET /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?afterSeq=… (sync after reconnect)
parts: Hold WebSocket connections; stateless apart from the connections.
user/device → gateway server (Redis), updated on connect/disconnect.
Assigns a per-conversation sequence number, stores the message, routes it.
Cassandra/HBase-style wide rows keyed by conversation, ordered by seq.
Undelivered messages per device until acked.
deep: Ordering and idempotency

The client sends a clientMsgId; the chat service de-duplicates on it and assigns a monotonically increasing seq per conversation (one partition owner per conversation). Clients display by seq and sync with "afterSeq" after reconnecting, so nothing is lost or duplicated.
Delivery and receipts

Delivered = the recipient device acked receipt; read = the app reported it was displayed. Each is a small message routed back to the sender. For groups, aggregate ("read by 12") rather than sending every receipt to every member.
Routing across gateways

The registry says user B is on gateway 417; the chat service sends there directly (or via a pub/sub topic per gateway). If B is offline, the message waits in B's inbox and a push notification wakes the app, which then syncs.
Groups
Fan-out on write for small groups (write to each member's inbox); store the message once and fan out references. For very large groups, members pull by seq.
followups: A gateway server crashes with 500K connections.
Clients reconnect to another gateway (with jittered backoff); the registry updates; they sync from their last seq. Nothing is lost because messages were stored before delivery.
How do you guarantee order in a group with senders on different servers?
A single sequencer per conversation (the partition owner), not per sender.
Last seen at scale.
Heartbeats update presence in Redis with TTL; fan out presence only to contacts with the chat open; batch and coarsen.
How does end-to-end encryption change the design?
The server stores and routes ciphertext; keys per device (Signal protocol); multi-device means encrypting per device.
How would you monitor it?
Connections per gateway, send-to-deliver latency, undelivered queue size, push success, reconnect storms.
mistakes: HTTP polling for new messages.
Ordering by timestamps from clients.
No acks, so messages are lost when a connection drops.
Fanning out every read receipt to every group member.
Forgetting multi-device delivery.
guide.say: "Clients hold WebSockets to gateways; a registry maps each device to its gateway; the chat service de-duplicates by client id, sequences per conversation, stores, then routes or queues for offline devices with push; acks drive delivered and read receipts; and reconnecting devices sync by sequence number."

model: conv_id, seq, msg_id, sender, body/ciphertext, ts

trade.chosen: Fan-out on write up to the group limit; pull for very large channels.
trade.flip: Broadcast channels with millions of members — pull.

Uses **acks** end to end so nothing is lost on dropped connections.

title: Route traffic to servers at exact percentages (and exact quotas)
statement: Design a system that distributes incoming requests across backend servers A, B and C at exactly 20%, 50% and 30% — exactly, not approximately. Then: add server D, which must receive exactly 1,000 requests per hour. Also: thousands of requests may arrive at once when they cannot all be processed — how do the rest wait? Requests arrive at many load-balancer instances.
why: Older (2019, 2022) but distinctive: "exactly" 20/50/30 and an exact hourly quota, plus global ids across 5 DCs.

variants.text: Distribute traffic to servers A, B, C at exactly the configured percentages (20/50/30), not approximately; then add server D receiving exactly 1,000 requests per hour. Also: thousands of simultaneous requests that cannot all be processed — how do the rest wait? And: assign new user ids in parallel, replicated across 5 data centres.
variants.note: Offer. Old, but unusual and Agoda-specific in style (follow-ups on the candidate's own resume project).

variants.text: A system with multiple servers running multiple test cases in parallel; the candidate proposed consistent hashing at the producer to spread work evenly. Kafka, SQL vs NoSQL and ALB/NLB came up.
variants.note: A related "spread work across servers" question; counted here.

guide.gist: From a 2019 Senior Bangkok offer, and related to a 2022 report on spreading test runs across servers. The trap is "exactly": random weighted choice is only approximately right, and **many load-balancer instances** each deciding locally drift apart. The answer is to be precise about **over what window** exactness holds, then use **deterministic smooth weighted round-robin per instance** plus **a shared counter or token allocation** for global exactness, and a **queue** for overflow.
clarify: Exact over what window — every 10 requests, every minute, cumulative?
Defines what "exact" can even mean; per-window exactness is achievable.
How many load-balancer instances?
One instance can be exact locally; many need coordination or partitioning.
Must a given user stick to one server?
Stickiness conflicts with exact splits — choose.
D's 1,000/hour: a minimum, a maximum, or both?
Exactly both → a quota that must be filled and capped.
What if a server is down?
Exactness must yield to availability — redistribute and say so.
numbers: 10K requests/s across 10 LB instances → 1K/s each.
D: 1,000 per hour ≈ 0.28/s — tiny next to the stream, so it is a quota, not a weight.
A shared counter for every request = 10K ops/s on Redis — feasible; token blocks reduce it 100×.
api: Config: PUT /v1/routing {weights: {A:20, B:50, C:30}, quotas: {D: {perHour: 1000}}}
LB internal: next() → server, using local smooth weighted round-robin + quota tokens
Overflow: requests beyond capacity go to a bounded queue with a deadline; 503 + Retry-After when it is full
parts: Holds weights and quotas; versioned; pushed to LBs.
Each runs smooth weighted round-robin — deterministic, exact per cycle of 10.
Allocates blocks of the global sequence (or quota tokens) to LB instances — global exactness.
Hands out D's 1,000 tokens per hour in small batches.
Bounded queue per server with deadlines; back-pressure.
Removes dead servers; logs deviations from the target split.
deep: Why random is not exact

Choosing A with probability 0.2 gives 20% only on average; over 100 requests you will see 14–26%. Smooth weighted round-robin (the nginx algorithm: add each weight to a current score, pick the highest, subtract the total from it) gives exactly 2 A, 5 B, 3 C in every 10 requests, interleaved (B A C B C B A B C B …).
Many LB instances

Each instance exact per 10 does not make the total exact at any moment (one instance may be mid-cycle). For global exactness: number requests globally — each LB takes a block of 100 sequence numbers from a coordinator (Redis INCRBY 100) and maps sequence n to a server by its position in the 10-cycle. Total is exact at every block boundary. Or partition traffic so each LB owns a fixed slice and is exact locally.
Exact quotas (D = 1,000/hour)

Treat D as a quota, not a weight: an allocator hands LBs batches of D-tokens (e.g. 10 at a time) and spreads them evenly over the hour; a request routed to D consumes a token; unused tokens are reclaimed near the end of the hour so exactly 1,000 are used if traffic exists.
Requests that cannot be served
A bounded queue per server with a deadline: if waiting longer than the deadline, fail fast (503 + Retry-After). Back-pressure to clients beats unbounded queues that time out anyway.
followups: Server B goes down.
Exactness yields: redistribute B's share by the remaining weights, log the deviation, and resume the exact split when B returns.
The coordinator (Redis) is down.
LBs fall back to local smooth round-robin — still exact per instance, approximate globally — and report it.
Requests have different costs.
Exact by request count may be unfair by load; weight by cost units instead, if that is the real goal.
Assign a new user id in parallel, replicated across 5 data centres (the same report's next question).
Avoid a global counter: give each data centre its own range or id prefix (DC id + local sequence), or Snowflake-style ids (time + DC + worker + sequence) — unique without coordination.
How would you monitor it?
Actual vs target share per server per window, quota consumption over the hour, queue depth and wait time, 503 rate.
mistakes: Random weighted choice and calling it exact.
Ignoring that several LB instances decide independently.
Treating D's 1,000/hour as a weight.
Unbounded queues for overflow.
Never stating the window over which exactness holds.
guide.say: "I'd define exactness per window, run smooth weighted round-robin on each balancer so every 10 requests split 2/5/3 exactly, get global exactness by allocating sequence blocks from a coordinator, model D as a quota of tokens allocated evenly across the hour, and protect servers with bounded queues and deadlines."

nfr: Low added latency (< 1 ms per decision)
cap: Local decisions, no per-request remote call

trade.chosen: Deterministic WRR locally, sequence blocks globally, quota tokens for D.
trade.flip: If ±2% is acceptable, random weighted choice per LB is simpler.

title: Ride-sharing app like Uber / Lyft
statement: Design a ride-sharing app like Uber or Lyft. Riders request a ride from a pickup to a destination; nearby drivers get the request and one accepts; both see each other's live location during the trip; the fare is calculated and paid at the end. Cover functional and non-functional requirements, the high-level design, the database, and deep dives.
why: Supplied by you; a standard question with geo-indexing and matching.

variants.text: "Design a ride sharing service such as Ola." (listed under the onsite system design section)
variants.note: A prep guide's list.

variants.text: Round 3 (system design): design a ride-sharing app like Uber or Lyft. FR, NFR, HLD, DB, deep dives; a couple of behavioural questions at the end.

guide.gist: Two hard parts: **a fast-changing geo index** (millions of drivers sending locations every few seconds, queried by "who is near this point?") and **matching without double-assigning a driver**. Everything else — trips, payment, ratings — is ordinary CRUD around a trip state machine.
clarify: How many active drivers and riders at peak, in how many cities?
Decides location update rate and geo-index sharding (by city/region).
How often do drivers send their location?
Every 4–5 s is typical → the write rate.
Matching: nearest driver, or best by ETA and other factors?
Nearest first; ETA-based is a deep dive.
Surge pricing, pooling, scheduled rides in scope?
Usually out of scope; mention as extensions.
Latency target for a match?
A few seconds.
numbers: 1M active drivers × one update / 4 s = 250K location writes/s.
Ride requests ~50K/min at peak ≈ 1K/s; each queries nearby drivers.
Locations are tiny (~50 bytes) and only the latest matters → keep them in memory (Redis geo), not in a database per update.
api: PUT /v1/drivers/me/location {lat, lng, heading} (every ~4 s, or over a WebSocket)
POST /v1/rides {pickup, dropoff} → {rideId, status: MATCHING}; GET /v1/rides/{id}
POST /v1/rides/{id}/accept (driver) → 200 or 409 already taken; WebSocket for live updates

Finds candidate drivers near the pickup, offers the ride, assigns exactly one.
Trip state machine: requested → matched → arrived → in progress → completed / cancelled.
WebSockets to riders and drivers for offers and live location.
Fare estimate, final fare, charge at the end.
deep: The geo index

Divide the map into cells (geohash or Uber's H3 hexagons). Each driver's latest location goes into its cell; "near the pickup" = the pickup cell plus its neighbours, then exact distance. Redis GEOADD/GEOSEARCH does this per city shard. Keep only the latest point; history goes to a log asynchronously.
Matching without double assignment

Offer the ride to the best few drivers. Assignment is a compare-and-set: the driver's state goes AVAILABLE → ASSIGNED only if still AVAILABLE (Redis WATCH/Lua or a conditional DB update), and the ride goes MATCHING → MATCHED only once. A second accept gets 409.
Live location during the trip
Driver updates flow through the location service and are pushed to the one rider over their WebSocket; a pub/sub channel per trip lets any gateway node deliver.
Hot spots and failures
Shard by city/region; split hot cells (an airport) further. If the location service loses a node, drivers re-send within seconds — it is soft state.
followups: Two riders' requests offered to the same driver.
The driver can accept one; the state CAS makes the second accept fail and that ride goes to the next candidate.
The driver's app loses connectivity mid-trip.
The trip continues server-side; the app buffers GPS and uploads later; fare uses the reconstructed route.
How do you compute ETA rather than straight-line distance?
A routing engine on the road graph (precomputed contraction hierarchies) with live traffic; use it to re-rank the top candidates only.
How do you scale location writes 10×?
More shards by cell, batch updates per gateway, reduce update frequency when a driver is idle.
How would you monitor it?
Time to match, match rate, location update lag, WebSocket connections, assignment conflicts, trip state anomalies.
mistakes: Writing every location update to a relational database.
Scanning all drivers to find the nearest.
Assigning a driver without an atomic state check.
One global geo index with no sharding.
Ignoring the cell-border problem (search neighbours).
guide.say: "Drivers stream locations into an in-memory, city-sharded cell index; a ride request searches the pickup cell and neighbours, offers to the best few, and assigns exactly one with a compare-and-set on driver and ride state; WebSockets carry live location; trips and payments are a durable state machine."

title: Doctor appointment booking application
statement: Design a doctor appointment booking application. Patients search doctors by specialty, location and availability, see open slots, and book, reschedule or cancel. Doctors and clinics manage their schedules (working hours, breaks, leave). Patients get reminders. Two patients must never get the same slot.
why: Supplied by you; booking slots without double booking — the same core as hotels.

variants.text: Create a doctor appointment booking application.

guide.gist: The same core as hotel booking, at a smaller scale: **slots as inventory**, booked with an **atomic conditional update**, plus schedule management (recurring rules → concrete slots), time zones, holds during payment, and **reminders**. Good answers keep it simple and correct, then cover the edge cases: rescheduling, doctor leave, no-shows.
clarify: Generate slots from rules, or do doctors create each slot?
Rules (Mon–Fri 9–5, 15-min slots) → materialise slots ahead.
Payment at booking?
Then a short hold before confirming.
Video consults, multiple clinics per doctor?
A slot belongs to a doctor and a location.
How far ahead can patients book?
Decides how many slots we materialise (e.g. 60 days).
Reminders: SMS, email, push; when?
24 h and 1 h before.
numbers: 100K doctors × 32 slots/day × 60 days ≈ 190M slot rows → shard by doctor_id, or keep per-doctor calendars.
1M bookings/day ≈ 12/s average, ~100/s peak — light writes.

deep: Taking a slot
UPDATE slot SET status = BOOKED, patient = ? WHERE slot_id = ? AND status = FREE — one row changes or the slot is taken. A unique index on (doctor_id, start_time) prevents duplicate slots.
Rules to slots
Store recurring rules; a job materialises slots 60 days ahead and extends daily. When a doctor adds leave, the job marks affected FREE slots unavailable and lists BOOKED ones for rescheduling.
Time zones
Store instants in UTC plus the clinic's time zone; display in the clinic's local time. Daylight-saving changes are handled by regenerating slots from rules in local time.
Reminders

On booking, schedule jobs at T−24 h and T−1 h (a delayed queue or a scheduler table scanned every minute). On cancel or reschedule, cancel the jobs; the job also re-checks the appointment status before sending.

The doctor goes on emergency leave tomorrow.

No-shows.
Mark no-show after the slot; policies (deposits, limits) per clinic.
How would you monitor it?
Booking success and conflict rate, reminder delivery rate, slot generation job health, search latency.

Generating slots on the fly for every search.

Sending reminders without re-checking that the appointment still exists.
Ignoring doctor leave and its effect on existing bookings.

title: Location-sharing app with time- and place-based sharing rules
statement: Design a location-sharing app (like Find My or Google Maps location sharing). Users share their live location with friends. A user can restrict sharing: only during certain hours (e.g. 9:00–18:00 on weekdays), only while they are inside or outside certain places (e.g. not while at home), or for a limited time ("for the next 2 hours"). Friends see a map of the people sharing with them.
why: Older (2024) but specific: sharing rules by time and by place make it a data-model question.

variants.text: Round 2: design a location-sharing app, focused on database design and sharing restrictions — one user restricting another by time and by location.
variants.note: Also supplied by you: "with time and location based sharing restrictions".

guide.gist: Reported with the focus on **database design and the sharing restrictions**. So the centre is a **rules model** — per (owner, viewer) grants with time windows, place conditions and expiry — and an **evaluation path** that is cheap enough to run on every location update or every read. The live-location part is standard (latest location in memory, fan-out to viewers).
clarify: Who evaluates the rules — on write (when the owner moves) or on read (when a friend looks)?
Decides where the cost lands; often both, with caching.
Place rules: circles (geofences) or named places?
Geofences as (lat, lng, radius) → point-in-circle checks.
Whose time zone defines "9–18"?
The owner's — store it with the rule.
Live updates or on-demand?
Push to viewers with the app open; otherwise last known on demand.
What does a viewer see when sharing is off — nothing, or last allowed location?
A privacy decision; default to nothing or a coarse "sharing paused".
numbers: 50M users, 10M sharing at any time, updates every 30 s when moving → ~330K writes/s.
Average 5 viewers per sharer → rule evaluations ~1.6M/s if done per viewer per update — evaluate per (owner, rule) once and fan out.
Latest location only in hot storage: 10M × 100 B = 1 GB.

deep: The data model for restrictions

share(owner_id, viewer_id, created_at, expires_at, active) plus conditions: time windows (days, start, end, owner tz) and place rules (place_id, mode: only_inside | never_inside). Partition by owner_id: every update needs the owner's grants together. A viewer index (viewer_id → owners) serves "who shares with me".
Evaluate once per update, not per viewer

When the owner moves, compute the place state once (which of my places am I in?) and the time state once; then each grant is a cheap boolean over those. Cache the owner's compiled rules in memory with the latest location.
Write-time vs read-time

Push path: evaluate on write and fan out only to allowed, online viewers. Pull path: on read, re-evaluate with current time (a time window may have closed since the last update). Expiry ("2 hours") is just expires_at checked on both paths, plus a sweeper.
Privacy defaults

title: Wallet and rewards ledger (store credit, loyalty cashback) with double-entry accounting
statement: Design a ledger for user balances at Agoda: store credit from refunds, cashback and loyalty rewards earned on stays, spent at checkout alongside a card. Rewards are pending until the stay completes, can expire, and can be clawed back if the booking is cancelled. Users must always see a correct balance; finance must be able to prove every balance.
why: One thin report (ledger calculation, Lead Backend 2025) plus your team's scope: coupons, refunds and store credit all post to a ledger.

variants.source: Taro — Lead Backend Engineer, India, Mar 2025, no offer (via search summary)
variants.text: Features discussed included ledger calculation, a notification system and a payment system.
variants.note: Thin: a search summary of one report; the exact question is not visible.

variants.source: Team scope (supplied by you, Nov 2026) — not counted
variants.text: Coupons, payments, refunds: every one of them posts to a ledger.
variants.note: Derived from the team's scope.

guide.gist: The core idea is **double-entry**: every movement is a transaction of balanced entries (debits = credits), **append-only**, so a balance is the sum of entries and can always be proved. On top: **pending vs available** buckets, **lots** with expiry dates spent oldest-first, **idempotent posting**, and a **cached balance** that is never the source of truth. The concurrency trap is two checkouts spending the same balance at once.
clarify: Is store credit real money (refunds) or a marketing reward?
Different accounts and accounting treatment; refunds may be withdrawable, rewards are not.
When does cashback become usable — at booking, check-out, or after a hold period?
Needs a PENDING bucket and a scheduled release.
Do rewards expire? Oldest first?
Lots with expiry dates and FIFO consumption.
Multi-currency balances?
One balance per currency, or one home currency with FX at spend time.
Can a balance go negative (clawback after it was spent)?
Decides whether clawback fails, goes negative, or is recovered later.
numbers: Tens of millions of members; ~500K bookings/day each posting 1–3 reward transactions → ~1M transactions/day, ~3M entries.
Balance reads: every checkout and every account page → ~5–10K reads/s at peak → cache the balance per user.
Spend at checkout: ~50/s peak, but two concurrent spends on one user must serialise.

POST /v1/ledger/transactions  Idempotency-Key {type: EARN|RELEASE|SPEND|REFUND|CLAWBACK|EXPIRE, entries:[{account, amount}], ref}

parts: The only writer. Validates balanced entries, idempotency, and invariants; append-only.
Per user: available, pending, held; system accounts: rewards expense, breakage, cash clearing.
Each credit is a lot with amount remaining and expiry; spends consume oldest lots first.

deep: Why double entry

A single 'balance' column can be changed by a bug with no trace. With entries, every change says where the money came from and went: SPEND debits user:available and credits clearing; EXPIRE debits user:available and credits breakage. The sum of all entries is zero by construction, so a nightly check proves the books.
Concurrent spends

Two tabs spend the same $50. Serialise per user: `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the user's balance row (or a conditional update `available >= amount` with a version), then insert entries in the same transaction. Partition by user so the lock is local; throughput per user is tiny, so the lock costs nothing.
Holds at checkout

Checkout places a hold (available → held) before charging the card. Payment succeeds → capture (held → spent); fails or times out → release. Same expiring-reservation shape as coupons, so the two compose in one checkout.
Pending, expiry and clawback

Cashback posts to pending at booking; a scheduler releases it after check-out plus a hold period. A cancellation before release reverses the pending entry. After release, if already spent, policy decides: recover from future credit (negative available allowed down to a floor) or write off — but always as an entry, never an edit.
followups: How do you show the balance fast?
A projection row updated in the same transaction plus a Redis cache invalidated on commit. Reads tolerate a second of staleness; spends always check the database row.
A reward was posted twice by a retried consumer.
Idempotency key = (source event id, type). The second post returns the first transaction.
Finance asks for the balance on 31 March at midnight.
Sum entries up to that timestamp — append-only makes point-in-time balances a query, not a restore.
1M lots expire at midnight.
The expiry job runs in batches by user partition, ahead of time for lots expiring soon; each expiry is one small transaction.
Currency?
A balance per currency; spending in another currency converts at a locked rate and posts the FX difference to an FX account.
mistakes: A mutable balance column with no entries.
Updating the Redis balance and the database separately.
Spending without a per-user lock or conditional update.
Deleting or editing entries to fix mistakes instead of posting reversals.
Ignoring expiry order (spending newest credit first leaves old credit to expire — users complain).
guide.say: "Every movement is a balanced, append-only transaction; balances are a projection updated in the same database transaction and cached for reads; spends lock the user's row; rewards move pending → available → held → spent through ordinary transactions, and a nightly check proves the sum is zero."
