title: Refunds and cancellations for bookings (partial refunds, coupons, chargebacks)
statement: Design the refund system for Agoda. A user cancels a hotel or flight booking (fully or partly) and is owed money according to the cancellation policy. The original payment may have used a card, a local wallet, store credit and a coupon together, in a different currency from the hotel's. Refunds go back through the original payment provider. Cover the flow, failures and retries, duplicate prevention, and how finance knows every refund is correct.
why: Not reported as its own question — derived from your team's scope (refunds by name). Prepare it as hard as the payment question.

variants.source: Team scope (supplied by you, Nov 2026) — not counted
variants.text: Your interviewing team owns coupons, payments, reconciliation and refunds.
variants.note: No candidate report names a refund design question at Agoda; this is derived from the team's scope. The 2026 Staff payment report included refunds as part of the payment question.

guide.gist: A refund is **a payment in reverse, with more ways to go wrong**: the amount is computed from a policy at a point in time, it must be split back across every **tender** the user paid with, the provider may be slow or reject it, and a chargeback may arrive for the same money. The answer is a **refund state machine** with an **idempotency key per refund**, a **refund calculator** that is a pure function of (booking, policy, time), **double-entry ledger** entries for every leg, and **reconciliation** against the provider's refund reports. Never refund more than was captured — that invariant is the question.
clarify: Is the refund amount decided by the cancellation policy at cancel time, or can an agent override it?
A pure calculator plus an audited override path with approval limits.
Multiple tenders — card + store credit + coupon? Which gets money back first?
A refund allocation order; coupons are usually restored or forfeited, not paid out as cash.
Same currency as charged, or the hotel's currency?
Always refund in the currency charged; FX gain/loss is booked separately.
Was the payment captured yet, or only authorised?
Before capture, a refund is a void (cheaper, instant). After, it is a real refund.
Do we also need money back from the hotel or airline?
Supplier recovery is a separate flow; the user is not made to wait for it.
numbers: ~500K bookings/day, ~15–20% cancelled → ~80–100K refunds/day ≈ 1/s average, ~20/s after an airline schedule change or a disaster.
Each refund ≈ 2–4 legs (card, wallet, coupon restore, fee) → ~300K ledger entries/day.
Provider refund p99 is seconds to accept, but settlement to the card takes 5–10 days → refunds stay 'in flight' for a week; the state machine must be long-lived.
api: POST /v1/bookings/{id}/cancellations  Idempotency-Key {items?, reason} → {cancellationId, refundQuote}
GET  /v1/bookings/{id}/refund-quote → {amount, currency, legs:[{tender, amount}], policy, validUntil}  (pure read)

Pure function: (booking, policy snapshot, cancel time, tenders) → refund legs. Versioned, testable, replayable.
State machine per refund: REQUESTED → APPROVED → SUBMITTED → SUCCEEDED / FAILED → RETRYING / MANUAL.
Card / wallet providers, store credit (internal ledger), coupon service (restore or forfeit).
Double-entry entries for every leg; the cap check (refunded ≤ captured) is enforced here.
Matches our refunds with provider refund reports; finds stuck, duplicated and missing refunds.
deep: Never refund twice, never refund too much

Two independent guards. The Idempotency-Key makes a retried request return the same refund. The **cap** makes a different request that would over-refund fail: in the same transaction that creates the refund, check `captured − refunded − pending ≥ amount` on the payment row with a version check. A user double-clicking, an agent issuing a goodwill refund, and an automatic schedule-change refund can all race; only the cap stops all three.
Splitting back across tenders

The calculator returns legs in a fixed allocation order — usually the reverse of how money came in: store credit first back to store credit, then card, and the coupon either restored (if the policy allows and it has not expired) or forfeited. Partial cancellation of one room of three allocates proportionally. Writing this as data plus a pure function means finance can read the rules and tests can replay last month's refunds.
Provider failures and the long tail

A provider can time out after accepting. The orchestrator stores the provider's idempotency key per leg and retries with the same key; a timeout is UNKNOWN, not FAILED, until the webhook or a status poll resolves it. Card expired or account closed → fall back to store credit or bank transfer with the user's consent, through a MANUAL state with an SLA.
Chargebacks against refunded money

A user may file a chargeback after we refunded. Link chargebacks to the payment, check refunded amount, and submit evidence automatically; ledger entries make the double loss visible the same day rather than at month end.
followups: The provider returns a timeout. Did the refund happen?
Unknown. Keep the state SUBMITTED_UNKNOWN, retry with the same provider idempotency key, and resolve from the webhook or a status poll. Never create a new refund for it.
An airline cancels 300 flights; 40,000 refunds in an hour.
Refunds go through a queue with per-provider rate limits; quotes are computed immediately so users see the amount, and money moves at the rate providers accept. Priority by travel date.
The user paid with a coupon worth $20. What do they get back?
Policy decides: restore the coupon if still valid, otherwise forfeit. Never pay a coupon out as cash — that turns a marketing cost into a cash leak.
Finance says refunds don't match the provider's report.
Daily reconciliation by provider refund id; mismatches are classified (missing on our side, missing on theirs, amount differs, duplicated) and opened as cases.
How do you get money back from the hotel?
A separate supplier-recovery flow: offset against the next payout to that hotel. The user's refund never waits for it.
mistakes: Refunding by calling the provider directly from the cancel API, with no state machine.
Treating a provider timeout as failure and issuing a second refund.
No cap check — two refund paths can both succeed.
Refunding in the hotel's currency instead of the currency charged.
Paying coupons out as cash.

title: Payment orchestration: 200+ payment methods across many providers, with routing and failover
statement: Agoda accepts cards and hundreds of local payment methods (wallets, bank transfers, buy-now-pay-later) in many countries, through several payment providers and acquirers. Design the orchestration layer: choose a provider for each payment to maximise approval rate and minimise cost, fail over when a provider degrades, and add a new method or provider without touching checkout.
why: Derived from your team's scope and Agoda's own 200+ payment methods article: one payment API over many providers.

variants.source: Agoda Engineering, "Supporting more than 200 payment methods globally" — not counted
variants.text: Agoda's payments engineering has written about supporting 200+ payment methods.
variants.note: An engineering article, not an interview report.

variants.source: Team scope (supplied by you, Nov 2026) — not counted
variants.text: The payments team owns the provider integrations.
variants.note: Derived from the team's scope.

guide.gist: Checkout should talk to **one payment API**; behind it, an **orchestrator** picks a **route** (provider + acquirer) per payment from **rules plus live health and approval-rate data**, calls it through a **provider adapter**, and keeps one **payment state machine** regardless of provider. The hard parts: **failover without double charging**, **asynchronous methods** (redirects, QR codes, bank transfers that complete hours later), and keeping **tokens portable** across providers. Agoda has written about supporting 200+ payment methods, and publicly works with orchestration and acquiring partners.
clarify: What are we optimising — approval rate, cost, or both?
A routing score combining both, per country and card type.
Can a declined payment be retried on another provider?
Only for soft declines and technical failures, never hard declines (stolen card).
Are cards tokenised by one provider or a network/vault token?
Provider tokens lock you in; a vault or network token makes failover possible.
Which methods are asynchronous?
Redirect and push methods need pending states and webhooks.
How fast must a new method launch?
Adapters + configuration rather than checkout code.
numbers: ~500K payments/day, ~60/s peak; each may try up to 2 routes → ~120 provider calls/s at worst.
+1% approval rate on billions in volume is worth far more than the whole system's cost — routing quality is the business case.
Provider health window: approval and error rates per route over the last 1–5 minutes, ~hundreds of routes.

GET  /v1/payment-methods?country&currency&amount → available methods (config-driven)
POST /webhooks/{provider}  (signed) → normalised events
parts: One contract for checkout; idempotency; returns next action for async methods.
Config: which methods in which countries, currencies, limits; drives the checkout UI.
Rules (country, BIN, currency, amount) + live scores (approval rate, latency, cost) → ordered list of routes.
One per provider: map requests, errors and webhooks into one internal model.
Stores network tokens / vault tokens so a card can be sent to more than one provider.
Streams outcomes per route; trips a circuit breaker on errors or approval drops.
deep: Routing as data

A route list is computed per payment: filter by rules (method supported, currency, 3-D Secure capability), then rank by a score = expected approval × value − cost, using the last few minutes of outcomes per route. A small share of traffic explores other routes so scores stay fresh. Rules and weights are configuration with an audit trail, rolled out like any risky config.
Failover without double charging

Retry on another route only when the first attempt is **known** not to have succeeded: a technical error before the provider accepted, or a soft decline. A timeout is unknown — query the first provider (status API with our idempotency key) before trying another. Each attempt is its own row under the payment, so at most one can reach CAPTURED; a late success on an abandoned attempt is voided.
Asynchronous methods

Wallets and bank transfers return an action (redirect, QR). The payment sits in PENDING_ACTION with an expiry; the webhook or a poll completes it. Booking confirmation waits on the payment state, and expiry releases inventory and coupons — the same expiring-reservation pattern again.
Adding a provider

An adapter implements one interface (authorise, capture, refund, void, status, parse webhook), passes a contract test suite against a sandbox, then takes 1% of eligible traffic behind a flag. Checkout never changes.
followups: Provider A's approval rate drops from 92% to 60% in five minutes.
The health monitor sees it per route; the circuit breaker moves traffic to the next route; alert the payments on-call. Keep a trickle to detect recovery.
We timed out on provider A. Retry on B?
Not yet — ask A for the status by our idempotency key. Only if A says not processed do we try B. Otherwise risk charging twice.
How do you prove the router helps?
Experiment: a holdout on static routing; compare approval rate and cost per country.
PCI scope?
Card data only in the vault / provider fields; the orchestrator handles tokens, so most services stay out of scope.
A local wallet is down in Indonesia.
Catalogue hides it for that country (health-driven config); users see other methods.
mistakes: Hard-coding provider choice in checkout.
Retrying on another provider after a timeout without checking the first.
Retrying hard declines elsewhere (fraud signal, scheme penalties).
Provider-specific tokens only — failover becomes impossible for saved cards.
Treating async methods like cards (no pending state, no expiry).

title: Paying hotels and suppliers: payouts and settlement (virtual cards and bank transfers)
statement: Agoda collects money from travellers and must pay hundreds of thousands of hotels and suppliers in many countries and currencies. Some are paid per booking with a virtual card the hotel charges, others by periodic bank transfer of a net amount (bookings minus commission, cancellations and adjustments). Design the payout system: what is owed, when, how it is paid, and how it is proven correct.
why: Derived from your team's scope and Agoda's public virtual-card programme: paying hotels is the other half of the money.

variants.source: J.P. Morgan case study — not counted
variants.text: Agoda pays hotel partners by virtual card and bank transfer, and moved to self-issued virtual cards (2020) in many currencies.
variants.note: Public business context, not an interview report.

variants.source: Team scope (supplied by you, Nov 2026) — not counted
variants.text: Payments and reconciliation include what Agoda owes and pays suppliers.
variants.note: Derived from the team's scope.

guide.gist: Two halves. **What is owed** is an accounting problem: a **payable** per booking from the contract (net rate, commission, taxes), adjusted by cancellations and recoveries, aggregated into a **statement** per supplier per period. **Paying it** is a payment problem: issue a **virtual card** per booking (limited to the amount and dates) or make a **bank transfer** of the net balance, idempotently, with **reconciliation** of what the hotel actually charged or received. Agoda has publicly described moving to self-issued virtual cards in many currencies.
clarify: Prepaid (we collect) or pay-at-hotel (hotel collects, we invoice commission)?
Opposite money flows; pay-at-hotel produces receivables, not payables.
Per-booking virtual card or periodic bank transfer — or both?
Per-booking issuance vs a batch settlement run.
When is a booking payable — at booking, check-in or check-out?
Decides the payable's due date and card validity window.
Which currency do we pay in?
The contract currency; FX exposure between collection and payout must be tracked.
How are cancellations after payout recovered?
Netting against future payouts, or a recovery request.
numbers: ~500K bookings/day → ~500K payables/day; a few hundred thousand suppliers.
Virtual cards: one per prepaid booking → hundreds of thousands issued per day, each with an amount cap and a validity window.
Bank transfers: weekly or monthly per supplier → a settlement run of ~100K+ transfers, batched to banks with cut-off times.
api: Internal: POST /v1/payables {bookingId, supplierId, amount, currency, dueAt, terms}  (idempotent on bookingId+version)
POST /v1/virtual-cards {payableId, amount, currency, validFrom, validTo} → {cardToken} (sent to the hotel via the extranet / channel)
POST /v1/settlement-runs {period, suppliers?} → runId;  GET /v1/suppliers/{id}/statements/{period}
parts: Turns booking events into payables from the contract; cancellations and amendments post adjustments.
Per-supplier account: payables, payments, recoveries — double entry, so the balance owed is provable.
Issues a card per booking with amount and date limits; tracks authorisations and settlements from the card network.
Periodic: computes net balance per supplier, creates payment instructions, sends bank files / API transfers.
Per period: every booking, adjustment and payment; what the hotel sees in the extranet.
Card charges vs payables (over/under-charge, early charge); bank confirmations vs instructions.
deep: Payable is computed, not typed

A payable is a pure function of the booking and the contract version at booking time: net rate, commission, taxes, currency. Amendments create a new version and post the difference. This gives one answer to 'what do we owe hotel X for booking Y' that finance, support and the hotel all see.
Virtual cards bound the risk

A card per booking, limited to the payable amount and valid from check-in, means a hotel cannot charge twice, early or too much without the card network declining it. Card network settlement files tell us what was actually charged; differences become cases. Cancelled before charge → close the card, no recovery needed.
Settlement runs must be idempotent

A run computes balances at a cut-off, creates one instruction per supplier with key (supplier, period), and sends them. If the run crashes halfway, re-running skips instructions already created. Bank rejections (wrong account, closed) move the instruction to a correction queue; the balance stays owed in the ledger.
Netting and recoveries

A cancellation after a bank payout posts a recovery; the next run nets it against new payables. If a supplier's balance stays negative past a threshold, collections takes over. All of it is entries in the supplier ledger, so the statement always reconciles.
followups: The hotel charges the virtual card twice.
The card's amount limit declines the second charge. If the limit allowed it (amendment), reconciliation flags the overcharge against the payable and opens a case.
The settlement run crashes after sending half the bank file.
Instructions are keyed by (supplier, period); re-run reuses existing ones and only sends what has no bank acknowledgement. The bank's own file id prevents double processing.
A booking is cancelled after we paid the hotel.
Post a recovery to the supplier ledger; net it in the next run.
Pay in the hotel's currency but we collected in USD?
Lock the rate at booking, record the payable in contract currency, post FX gain/loss at payout.
How do you monitor it?
Payables created vs bookings, cards issued vs used, unmatched card charges, settlement run progress, bank rejections, supplier balance ageing.
mistakes: Computing what is owed at payout time from current contract data (contracts change).
One shared corporate card for all hotels.
A settlement run that is not idempotent.
Waiting for supplier recovery before refunding the traveller.
No per-supplier ledger — balances become spreadsheets.

title: Multi-currency: showing, charging and settling prices in different currencies
statement: A user in Japan books a hotel in Thailand priced in THB by the supplier, sees the price in JPY, may pay in JPY or USD, and Agoda pays the hotel in THB days later. Design how prices are converted, which rate is used when, how the user is protected from the price changing between search and payment, and how FX gains and losses are accounted for.
why: Derived from your team's scope: every Agoda payment crosses currencies, and reconciliation fails on cents.

variants.source: Team scope (supplied by you, Nov 2026) — not counted
variants.text: Payments, refunds and reconciliation all cross currencies at Agoda.
variants.note: Derived from the team's scope; FX also appears as a clarifying question in the reported payment and reconciliation questions.

guide.gist: Separate **three currencies** (supplier, display, charge) and **three moments** (search, booking, payout). Rates come from a **rate service** with versioned snapshots; search uses cached rates; booking **locks a rate** (stored with the booking) so the amount charged equals the amount shown; payout uses the then-current rate, and the difference goes to an **FX gain/loss account**. Money is stored as **integer minor units with a currency**, never floats, and rounding rules are explicit per currency.
clarify: Which currency do we charge — the user's, the supplier's, or their choice?
Decides who takes FX risk and whether we need the card's currency.
How long is a shown price guaranteed?
A quote validity window (e.g. 15–30 minutes) with a locked rate.
Rate source and update frequency?
A provider feed every few minutes; a markup per currency pair.
Do we hedge?
Treasury concern; the system must report net exposure per currency.
Refunds — at the original or the current rate?
The original charged amount in the charged currency, always.
numbers: ~40+ display currencies × 40+ supplier currencies → a ~1,600-pair matrix, refreshed every few minutes — tiny.
Search converts millions of prices per second → conversion must be an in-memory multiply, not a call.
500K bookings/day each store one locked rate snapshot id.

POST /v1/quotes {itinerary, displayCurrency, chargeCurrency} → {quoteId, amounts, rateVersion, validUntil}

Each instance holds the latest snapshot in memory; converts for display only.

deep: Money representation

Amounts as integers in minor units plus a currency code (JPY has 0 decimals, THB 2, some 3). Conversion uses decimal arithmetic and one rounding rule (banker's or half-up) applied once at the end. Floats lose cents across millions of bookings, and reconciliation fails on exactly those cents.
Locking the rate

The price a user saw must be what they pay. The quote stores the rate version and computed amounts; payment charges the quote. If the quote expires, re-quote and show the new price if it changed. Without this, a rate update between page load and Pay creates mismatched amounts and support tickets.
Where FX risk lands

Between charging in JPY today and paying THB on check-out, rates move. The supplier ledger records the payable in THB; at payout the actual conversion is posted and the difference against the locked rate goes to FX gain/loss. Treasury reads net exposure per currency from the ledger to hedge.
Rate snapshots are immutable
Every snapshot has a version and is never changed. Any amount can be recomputed exactly from its inputs and the version — essential for reconciliation and disputes.
followups: The rate feed is down.
Keep serving the last snapshot with an age limit; after the limit, widen the markup or stop selling in affected pairs. Alert.
The user's card is in EUR but we charge JPY.
The issuer converts (dynamic currency conversion choices aside); our amount is still JPY. Refund in JPY too.
Why not convert at payment time?
The user would pay a different amount than shown. Lock at quote.
How do you reconcile with the provider?
Provider reports amounts in the charged currency; match in minor units — no FX involved at that step.
Rounding: three rooms, total doesn't equal the sum.
Convert the total once, allocate the rounding remainder to one line deterministically.
mistakes: Floats for money.
Recomputing the price at payment with a newer rate.
Refunding at today's rate.
Mutable rate tables — no way to reproduce an old amount.
Calling a rate service per search result.
